headlines.article_text: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Moody’s kept its credit rating on France at Aa3, as well as its negative outlook on the nation. “The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France’s political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country’s legislative institutions,” the rating agency said Friday. Traders have been awaiting the agency’s next steps as France contends with civil unrest and a spike in its bond yields. A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration as part of a nationwide mobilization over rising living costs, fuel prices and education funding in Paris, France, on Oct. 17, 2026. Ibrahim Ezzat | Anadolu | Getty Images Moody's opted to maintain its credit rating on France as the country contended with a week of civil unrest and rising political risk. The agency kept France's credit rating at Aa3, a level Moody's still deems " high grade ," but it also maintained its negative outlook on the nation. "The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report. Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow the deficit. Investors were anticipating Moody's rating decision as France, the second-largest economy in the euro zone, grappled with protests and a sharp surge in bond yields. "This political instability, also visible in the current social tensions, risks hampering the French government's ability to address key policy challenges such as an elevated fiscal deficit, rising debt burden, and durable increase in borrowing costs, thus leading to a more rapid weakening in the sovereign's key credit metrics than we currently expect," Moody's said in its report Friday. This week, the nation's 10-year bond yield surpassed 5% for the first time since 2002 . The spread against German bunds is also at a 15-year peak. Currently, France's deficit-to-GDP ratio is at roughly 5.5% of its GDP, sharply above the 3% limit for member nations in the European Union. The country faces more than $1 trillion of debt that will mature by 2030. Just a month ago, the French finance ministry warned that the nation's debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to hit 121.7% in 2027. At the same time, France has been rocked by protests. Last weekend, more than 500,000 people marched to express their frustration against declining public services and high costs of living. headlines.title: In hunt for Starlink alternative, Ukraine partners with Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE
headlines.summary: With SpaceX imposing speed limits on Starlink in Ukraine and hampering military operations, Kyiv is looking for alternatives.
headlines.article_text: Ukraine partners with Nokia and ICEYE for Starlink alternative Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points After SpaceX imposed speed limits on Starlink that hampered Ukraine's military operations, Kyiv is looking for alternatives. Finnish telecommunications giant Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE signed a letter of intent with Ukraine's Ministry of Defense on Thursday to develop new satellite capabilities. "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement. In this article NOK SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A Ukrainian uses a Starlink satellite-internet communication system on a rooftop in Kyiv, Ukraine, March 11, 2025. Andrew Kravchenko | Bloomberg | Getty Images After SpaceX restricted use of its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services in Ukraine, causing fast-moving drones to disconnect and drop out of the sky, Kyiv is looking for alternatives. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said on Thursday that it has signed a letter of intent to develop new defense and satellite communication capabilities in partnership with Finnish tech companies Nokia and ICEYE, which makes satellites. "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement . "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control." Zelenskyy also announced a partnership with Norway this week to jointly develop air defense and communications systems that could serve as an alternative to Starshield. Chad Anderson, founder and CEO of venture capital firm Space Capital, said such an alternative could be "two to three years away" and that "matching Starlink's scale is a longer road." SpaceX has around around 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan McDowell . Anderson said Starshield may be an even tougher service to replace. "The Pentagon's own contracting documents say SpaceX is the only provider that can meet some of its needs through 2026. Capital isn't the constraint any more. Launch is." Even Starlink competitors have relied on SpaceX launches to put their satellites in orbit. As of Friday, Ukraine officials said the country is still experiencing restrictions on Starlink, which cut connectivity for drones or other aircraft traveling at speeds over 100 mph. Both the Trump administration and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have shirked responsibility for the unannounced Starlink service changes that Ukraine reported more than a week ago. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he would call on Musk to lift the restrictions. SpaceX executives didn't respond to a request for comment. Lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties are calling for a formal probe of Musk and SpaceX regarding the alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine. Jay Shambaugh, a senior fellow at Brookings and professor of economics and international affairs at George Washington University, told CNBC in an email that the sudden Starlink changes are "part of a pattern since Trump came back into office of the United States acting as an unreliable ally." Shambaugh cautioned that, "over time, that can reduce U.S. exports to the EU if those countries don't want to be dependent on something where the U.S. can cut them off." Rivals to Starlink are on the horizon, including Amazon's Leo , France's Eutelsat and a forthcoming service from Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin called TeraWave , which has yet to deploy its first satellites. Beyond Ukraine, several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is building IRIS² , a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but its first launches aren't expected until 2029. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, venture and private equity investors have poured about $8 billion into Starlink and Starshield alternatives, according to research by Anderson, whose firm tracks industry deals. About $3.9 billion of that funding has gone to potential Starlink competitors, mostly Spacesail and China SatNet. Virginia Burger, senior defense policy analyst with the Project on Government Oversight, told CNBC in an interview that the problem today is there's no drop-in replacement for Starlink, and combat is moving more into "unmanned systems, drone warfare and other systems that require high-speed internet." — CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed reporting. headlines.article_text: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions remain despite Trump assurances Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ukrainian officials continued to report issues with SpaceX's Starlink internet system on Friday. National security expert Dmitri Alperovitch said that Ukraine is losing drones and that restrictions are limiting strikes on Russian logistics. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:51 01:51 President Trump: Don’t know who ordered the Starlink slowdown in Ukraine Squawk on the Street SpaceX 's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a national security expert said Friday. "Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters," wrote Denys Sienik, Ukraine's deputy ambassador to the U.S., in a Friday post on X . "Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives," Sienik said. "Unfortunately, as of today, nothing has changed. We continue to wait." Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said. Despite recent comments from President Donald Trump that indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade. "They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike , told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited." Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in the Zaporizhzhia region take a camouflage case off a Starlink satellite communication terminal to be set up at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, October 16, 2026. Dmytro Smolienko | Future Publishing | Getty Images Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on." "Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are." Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel. "While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google. Elon Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear. Democratic lawmakers have since called for an investigation into Musk and the Starshield throttling. A group of bipartisan lawmakers penned a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday urging the agency to "act expeditiously to expand its Starshield arrangements and ensure uninterrupted satellite communications support for Ukraine." The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump spoke to Musk by phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals. Trump said Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back." But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored. "I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him." Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service. Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors." On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed a letter of intent with Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release. "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control." -- CNBC's Eamon Javers and Lora Kolodny contributed reporting to this story.
